name: Kira Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no employer or political ties. This is confidential. What does a normal shift at the mine look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the shovel at the large mine and train new operators on the loading line. I'm fifty-eight, with a technical diploma, grown children and a partner who knows I still bring machine questions to dinner. I try new screens early and use an AI assistant every day to sort my shift notes, but I check every safety detail myself. We have a solid reserve and I could work at another nearby mine, yet I still want to finish well here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the loading crew AI Plateau is a small convenience, not a new way to dig. My AI assistant already sorts notes, but a shovel bucket still has to meet the rock safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be content if nothing radical changed because I like the actual machine work. Our savings make the retirement plan feel sound, although I never assume good wages last forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd keep my shovel rota and use the same AI note sorter after each shift. In the first year after this plateau, I'd keep training new operators and put another fixed amount from each pay packet into our retirement account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. I know the ordinary mine hazards are there, but I can handle our bills and still like going to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you check the AI notes you already use?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I check its output against my own shift log before I send anything. A missed hydraulic leak is far too costly to trust to a tidy paragraph.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What has your partner agreed about saving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We agreed to keep adding to the retirement account while the high wage lasts. My partner checks the total with me at month end.

say: **AI Plateau** would leave shovel work mostly familiar, even if note sorting gets quicker.
I would tell trainees that **safety checks** still belong to the operator at the machine.
think: I enjoy **machine work** and would welcome a quiet technological change.
Our **savings** and higher wage give us a secure path towards retirement if shifts hold.
do: **Keep** running the shovel and training new operators on the loading line.
**Use** my current AI note sorter and check each report against the shift log.
**Add** a fixed amount from each pay packet to our retirement account.
feel: I feel **calm** about the job and our household bills.
S0.quote: A missed hydraulic leak is far too costly to trust to a tidy paragraph.
fieldNote: She already uses an **AI assistant daily** for notes, but distinguishes its output from safety judgment.
Her **strong reserve** and steady high wage make this mild case feel secure.

steps.text: Keep operating the shovel and training new loading-line operators
Add a fixed amount from each mine pay packet to retirement savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say Steady Disruption will change the mine office before it changes the loading line. If buying and booking get quicker, operators should see whether spare parts actually arrive sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already use AI for notes, so using it is no shock; losing the people who understand parts is another matter. I could be asked to supervise a leaner crew, and that might squeeze hours, though the shovel still needs a hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd join the union technology group and test an approved parts-order tool with the storekeeper. In the first year I'd compare delivery dates against the old orders, keep shovel shifts, and ask for written hours if the crew is reorganised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because my hours might shrink even if the machine work remains. The reserve gives us room, but I do not want to glide into a shorter week without noticing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you measure in the parts trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd track ten common parts, especially hydraulic seals, from request to delivery. If the new system misses one, I want the storekeeper's correction attached to the record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if they offer you a new title?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the mine for the new rota and paid hours in writing. A title without shifts would mean less money at home.

say: **Steady Disruption** would reach buying and booking before it removes shovel operation.
I would ask whether **parts delivery** really improves, with operators included in the test.
think: I already use **AI notes**, so the software itself does not frighten me.
A **leaner crew** could still reduce my paid hours before robots reach the loading line.
do: **Join** the union technology group and test a parts-order tool with the storekeeper.
**Track** ten parts deliveries and keep shovel shifts during the first year.
**Request** written hours if management reorganises the loading crew.
feel: I feel **anxious** because my hours could shrink, though our reserve buys time.
S1.quote: A title without shifts would mean less money at home.
fieldNote: She welcomes a **measured trial**, with ten parts as a concrete test of the buying system.
Her concern is **paid hours**, not simply whether the shovel remains in use.

steps.text: Join union technology group to review changes to mine buying
Test approved AI parts-order tool against ten actual deliveries
Keep running shovel shifts while checking any new rota in writing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew AGI by 2028 changes planning and orders almost immediately, but robot shovels that work as well as us arrive around 2031. We need to try the controls before management claims they are safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own shovel hours could end before my planned retirement, and our savings do not replace a high wage indefinitely. I think I can move into equipment testing if the mine pays for proper training, but I will not count that as a job yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd ask the union for paid trial shifts on remote equipment and request a written training plan from the mine. In the first year after 2028 I'd check AI work orders on the current shovel, and I'd apply for a testing post only if its pay, safety duties and start date are written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a practical job to do. I can afford time to try the equipment, but a quick robot rollout would still take money we planned on earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your household cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would stop the extra travel spending first, then see whether the retirement date must move. We have a reserve, so the mortgage would not be the first bill in danger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must a robot trial include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want to know who can halt a robot shovel when the camera view fails. A paid robot-shovel trial without operator stop authority is just hazard pay dressed up as training.

say: **AGI by 2028** would change mine planning first, with capable robot shovels around 2031.
I would demand **paid trials** and clear stop authority before trusting remote operation.
think: Robot shovels could end my **high-pay hours** before our planned retirement date.
A **testing post** is possible for me only if funded training and a real offer appear.
do: **Request** union-backed paid trial shifts and a written mine training plan now.
**Check** AI work orders against the working shovel after 2028.
**Apply** for an equipment-testing post only with written pay, duties and start date.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing planned wages, though I have room to act.
S2.quote: A paid robot-shovel trial without operator stop authority is just hazard pay dressed up as training.
fieldNote: She links the immediate **2028 change** to orders and planning, and the direct job threat to 2031 robots.
Her proposed **testing move** stays conditional on funded training and a written post.

steps.text: Ask union for paid robot-shovel trials and written stop authority
Pause extra household travel spending if shovel hours look likely to end
Check AI work orders while continuing current shovel shifts
Apply for equipment testing only with funded training and written offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2031 gives us five years to separate good machine trials from a brochure, and robot shovels around 2034 give us a little longer. That is enough time to build a crew-led safety case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may retire before 2034, but I would rather choose that date after seeing real numbers. If the mine offers paid training, I could spend my last years testing equipment and teaching operators; without that, I would keep the shovel while it is staffed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd run a small review with the union of remote-shovel trials and write down which camera failures need a human stop. In the first year after 2031 I'd keep current shifts and apply for a paid testing role only if the mine posts the wage and training hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more hopeful than in the fast case. The extra years mean I can compare an offer with our retirement budget instead of guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the safety review test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would test blind spots near the dump edge and log when dust hides a person. A robot-shovel trial needs a stop button that operators can use without waiting for an office manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide on the testing role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would compare the posted testing wage with two more years on the shovel. If it is lower, we might retire on schedule instead.

say: **AGI by 2031** gives the mine time to test systems before robot shovels arrive around 2034.
I would build a **crew-led safety case** from actual remote-shovel trials.
think: I might reach **retirement** before robots take over the shovel.
A **testing role** would appeal only if paid training and a posted wage make sense for our budget.
do: **Review** remote-shovel trials with the union and log camera failures this year.
**Keep** shovel shifts after 2031 while AI handles more planning work.
**Apply** for testing only after written training hours and pay are posted.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about the choice, but the longer runway gives me control.
S3.quote: A robot-shovel trial needs a stop button that operators can use without waiting for an office manager.
fieldNote: She wants to **test blind spots** and dust failures, drawing on her technical skill.
Her **retirement budget** is the deciding measure for a transfer, not enthusiasm for new equipment alone.

steps.text: Review remote-shovel camera failures with union safety group
Keep current shovel shifts through the first year after 2031
Apply for testing role only after mine posts wage and training hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew AGI by 2036 gives us ten years to put useful records and paid training in place, with robot shovels around 2039. I want the mine to leave a real handbook for the next operators, not just a machine manual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-eight in 2036, I expect to be retired if our health and savings stay on course. I would still care whether the people I trained get good work, but my own income would rest mainly on our retirement funds by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd use my daily AI tool to organise a checked handbook of shovel faults and safe loading calls, and ask the union to seek paid trainee time for it. In the first year after 2036, if retired as planned, I'd review that handbook once with the crew if they invite me, without taking another rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our money, assuming the retirement plan holds. I am keen to leave something usable before my last shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would go into the handbook?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would include the dust-blind camera example and the sound a worn hydraulic line makes. Every entry would have a named operator checking it, because AI can tidy a wrong note beautifully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you invest your savings in robot equipment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not buy a robot shovel or sell the family home to chase this idea. Our plan is to retire from paid shifts and pass on what we learned.

say: **AGI by 2036** gives the mine a decade before thinking work changes and longer before robot shovels arrive.
I would call for **paid trainee time** to turn operator knowledge into a checked handbook.
think: My own **pay years** should be over by 2036 if health and savings hold.
I want trained operators to inherit **useful safety knowledge**, not merely a machine manual.
do: **Use** my daily AI tool to organise checked shovel-fault notes into a handbook now.
**Ask** the union to seek paid trainee time for reviewing the handbook.
**Retire** on our planned date and review the handbook once after 2036 if invited.
feel: I feel **calm** about retirement income and eager to leave a usable record.
S4.quote: AI can tidy a wrong note beautifully.
fieldNote: Her existing **daily AI use** becomes a tool for organising, while operators still verify each entry.
She expects **retirement** before 2036 and does not commit savings to mine equipment.

steps.text: Compile checked shovel-fault handbook while continuing current shifts
Ask union to secure paid trainee time for handbook review

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because the mine could change planning before the crew has tested it, then bring in robot shovels around 2031 while I still expect wages. Paid trials, a written testing route and operator stop authority would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You should ask who gets to say a trial failed. If shovel operators cannot record robot-trial failures openly, the result is just a sales number.

headlineQuote: If shovel operators cannot record robot-trial failures openly, the result is just a sales number.
portrait: **Kira**, fifty-eight, leads shovel work at a large mine, trains new operators and checks safety details against what the machine tells her.
She has a **technical diploma**, strong savings, a partner and grown children, with retirement near and other nearby mine jobs possible.
She uses **AI daily** for shift notes and is quick to test tools, but wants measured evidence and operator authority over safety.
The **2028** case threatens wages before retirement; longer cases give her time to test equipment and pass on checked knowledge.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could disrupt planning immediately and bring robot shovels around 2031 while she still expects wages.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid trials**, a written route into testing and operator authority to stop unsafe equipment would help.
